britannica.headword: CYNANCHE MALIGNA, or PUTRID SORE THROAT
britannica.rawText:
CYN                    [ 612 ]                    CYN

CYMBAL, a muſical inſtrument of braſs, hollow and round.
  CYNANCHE MALIGNA, or PUTRID SORE THROAT, a diſeaſe in
which the throat and tonfils are covered with ulcers
and with ſloughs of a whitiſh or aſh colour, attended
with fever, great weakneſs, and a fetid breath. It is
contagious, and often appears as an epidemic; and it is
moſt fatal to children, many of whom it carries off in
a few days.
  It differs from the common inflammatory quinſy, in
which the throat is red and ſwelled but without
ſloughs, and which yields to bleeding; whereas in this
diſeaſe bleeding is very hurtful. Dr Fothergill of Lon-
don publiſhed an account of this diſeaſe in 1748, and
it has ſince been deſcribed by Dr Huxham and Dr Cullen.
  The cauſe is ſuppoſed to be a putrid ferment,
received from the air or from the breath of the ſick,
which corrupts the humours and produces a gangrene of
the parts. The cure conſiſts in ſupporting tbe ſtrength
with Peruvian bark and wine, and in cleanſing the
ulcers with gargles of capſicum, or of vinegar and
honey.
  CYNIC, a philoſopher of the ſect of Diogenes.

passages.section: CYNANCHE MALIGNA, or PUTRID SORE THROAT
passages.text: The cure consists in supporting the strength with Peruvian bark and wine, and in cleansing the ulcers with gargles of capsicum, or of vinegar and honey.
Diphtheria is an infection caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Symptoms often come on gradually, beginning with a sore throat and fever.
In severe cases, a grey or white patch called a pseudomembrane forms in the throat. It can block the airway and cause a barking cough as in croup.
Diphtheria usually spreads between people by direct contact or through the air. Most of the harm comes from a toxin that the bacterium makes, which can also damage the heart and nerves.
Before vaccination, diphtheria was a major cause of death in children. The disease kills between 5 and 10 percent of those infected.
Treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics such as erythromycin or penicillin.

The French physician Pierre Bretonneau named the disease in the 1820s, from the Greek word for leather, after the tough membrane in the throat. Edwin Klebs and Friedrich Loeffler identified the bacterium in 1883 and 1884, and Emil von Behring developed an antitoxin in the 1890s.
A diphtheria vaccine is effective and is usually given together with tetanus and pertussis vaccines.

reasons: The old headword names the disease by its signs, but the description matches diphtheria: sloughs in the throat, high death rate in children, epidemics.
Rare terms appear in both: sloughs and membrane, fetid breath, croup-like signs, antitoxin history.
Scarlet fever also scores, because some 18th-century accounts of the ulcerous sore throat may describe it.

alignments.label: Sloughs in the throat

britannica.quote: covered with ulcers and with sloughs of a whitish or ash colour

wikipedia.quote: a grey or white patch called a pseudomembrane forms in the throat

alignments.note: Same sign in new words. The sloughs of 1797 are the pseudomembrane of today.

alignments.label: Fatal to children

britannica.quote: it is most fatal to children

wikipedia.quote: a major cause of death in children

alignments.note: Both texts say children suffered most. The fact did not change.

alignments.label: Contagious

britannica.quote: It is contagious, and often appears as an epidemic

wikipedia.quote: usually spreads between people by direct contact or through the air

alignments.note: Both say it passes from person to person. Wikipedia names the routes.

alignments.label: Not the common quinsy

britannica.quote: It differs from the common inflammatory quinsy

wikipedia.quote: a grey or white patch called a pseudomembrane

alignments.note: The 1797 entry uses the sloughs to tell the two apart, and so does the modern sign. Inference: the quinsy of the period is close to what Wikipedia calls a peritonsillar abscess.

alignments.label: Fothergill, 1748

britannica.quote: Dr Fothergill of London published an account of this disease in 1748

alignments.note: Wikipedia does not name Fothergill. Inference: some 18th-century epidemics of ulcerous sore throat may have mixed diphtheria with scarlet fever.

alignments.label: Putrid ferment

wikipedia.quote: caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. A bacterium causes the disease, not a ferment from putrid air.

alignments.label: Gangrene of the parts

britannica.quote: corrupts the humours and produces a gangrene of the parts

wikipedia.quote: Most of the harm comes from a toxin that the bacterium makes

alignments.note: The 1797 entry saw dead tissue in the throat. Wikipedia explains it by a toxin, which can also harm the heart and nerves.

alignments.label: Bark, wine and capsicum

britannica.quote: supporting the strength with Peruvian bark and wine

wikipedia.quote: Treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Antitoxin came in the 1890s and antibiotics later. Bark and capsicum gargles do not act on the infection.

alignments.label: Vaccine
alignments.note: The 1797 entry has no prevention. The vaccine made the disease rare where it is used.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry think caused the putrid sore throat?
How was the disease treated in 1797 and how is it treated now?

What did the 1797 entry think caused the.answer: It blamed a putrid ferment taken in from the air or from the breath of the sick [B5]. Wikipedia says a bacterium, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, causes it [W1], and that most of the harm comes from the toxin the bacterium makes [W3]. The 1797 entry was right that the breath of the sick passes it on [B5] [W3].

How was the disease treated in 1797 and.answer: In 1797 the cure was Peruvian bark and wine, with gargles of capsicum or of vinegar and honey [B6]. Today treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics [W5], and a vaccine prevents the disease [W7].
